quizzes.title: Mergers, Exceptions and Member Categories
quizzes.passage: The anti-defection framework exists to discourage legislators from switching sides. The rules sit in a schedule of the Constitution and cover members of both Parliament and State legislatures. Their aim is to keep governments stable and to make legislators accountable for their conduct. Not every departure is treated the same way, however. The law treats independent members and nominated members differently, depending on when they choose to join a party. Political parties enforce discipline through whips, which direct members how to vote, and the law links defiance of those whips to possible loss of membership. The framework also allows whole groups of members to combine with another party under certain conditions, a feature critics say can encourage large-scale movement between parties. Decisions on these cases are taken by the presiding officer of each house, and courts review those decisions in limited ways. Judges have stressed that such decisions should not be delayed indefinitely, while commentators continue to question whether presiding officers can act impartially when they belong to the ruling party. The debate reflects a wider tension between stable government and the independence that individual legislators may want to exercise.

quizzes.title: Deciding Authority and Review
quizzes.passage: Once a disqualification petition is filed against a legislator, the central question becomes who decides it. The Constitution gives this power to the presiding officer of the house to which the member belongs, rather than to a court or to the executive. Critics argue that this arrangement places a significant power in the hands of someone who is often a member of the ruling party, which raises concerns about partisanship. Courts can step in, but generally only after the presiding officer has issued a decision, so the timing of judicial intervention is a recurring concern. Petitions can remain pending for long periods, and that delay can shape the stability of a government long before a final verdict is reached. Judges have said such decisions should be taken within a reasonable timeframe, although deadlines are not always met in practice. A decision may be reviewed by a court on specific grounds, such as when it violates a constitutional requirement, reflects bad faith, or is so unreasonable that no proper authority could have reached it. The procedure also has to respect basic fairness, which means the affected member must be heard. Such review is an important safeguard, yet it does not replace the initial role of the presiding officer in the process.

quizzes.title: Reserves Under Pressure
quizzes.passage: India's foreign exchange reserves have come under visible pressure in recent months, and this has raised concern about the country's external position. The reserves are external assets held by the Reserve Bank of India, and they act as a buffer when the economy faces outside shocks. They also help the country pay for essential goods such as crude oil and fertilisers. When inflows of foreign currency exceed outflows, the balance of payments strengthens the reserves and supports the rupee. When outflows rise, the reserves can shrink and the currency can weaken. Several forces added to the outflows in 2026. Crude oil prices have been volatile, which raises the energy import bill. Demand for gold imports has also reached record levels. The central bank has been active in the market, intervening to defend a rupee that was weakening. The Prime Minister has urged citizens to limit non-essential spending on gold purchases, overseas travel and fuel. The aim is to protect currency stability and reduce capital outflows. Experts caution, however, that overly strict controls could stifle manufacturing and broader economic growth. They argue that the country must protect its financial security without damaging its industrial base, and balancing these two goals is the central challenge for policymakers in the months ahead.

quizzes.title: Import Pressure Check
quizzes.passage: India's external payments depend heavily on what the country imports. Energy is among the largest of these imports, and India relies on foreign suppliers for most of its crude oil. When oil prices move sharply, the import bill changes with them, which affects the trade balance and the demand for dollars. Gold is another major import. Household purchases of gold do not create productive assets in the way that official reserves do, so heavy gold buying adds to the strain on the current account. Fertiliser is a third pressure point. Imported inputs such as urea and ammonia have risen sharply in price, and the government must decide how to respond. It can pass the higher costs on to consumers, which carries a risk of inflation, or it can absorb the costs itself. A weaker rupee adds to the problem, because it makes every imported good more expensive in rupee terms. Outflows also arise from personal spending abroad, such as foreign travel and overseas weddings. Each of these pressures feeds the others, and the economy has to weigh short-term relief against long-term health. Understanding which imports drive the outflow of foreign exchange is the first step in judging how much pressure the economy faces. Policy choices in this area therefore matter a great deal for households and businesses.

Regions also differ greatly, and journalists in some parts of the world face far greater danger than others. quizzes.title: History of the Indian Press
quizzes.passage: Printing reached India through European trading companies, and for a long time newspapers were produced by colonial interests and Indian reformers alike. Colonial governments were uneasy about printed criticism. At different times they introduced rules to control what could be published, and some of these rules fell hardest on publications written in Indian languages. Even so, Indian editors kept bringing out weeklies that promoted social reform and nationalist ideas. Reformers used the press to challenge customs and argue for change in society. Over time, the limits on the press became a question for the courts and the constitution. Debates about press freedom focused on how expression could be balanced with public order and the rights of others. Later, statutory and non-statutory bodies were set up to watch over journalism and protect editorial standards, while professional associations of editors took up the defence of journalists' rights. Studying this history explains why modern India treats press freedom as important yet not absolute, and why the state and the press continue to debate where the limits should lie. The sequence of laws and institutions shows a long pattern in which governments tried to restrict the press while journalists sought wider freedom.

quizzes.passage: Logistics performance across India's States and Union Territories is measured through LEADS, a national index that benchmarks each State and UT on common parameters. Excellence and innovation in the sector are recognised through a separate set of awards called LEAPS, which were conferred alongside the report. The LEADS framework takes inspiration from an international benchmark, the Logistics Performance Index of the World Bank. That global index analyses differences between countries in customs procedures, logistics costs and infrastructure quality. The national and global tools therefore differ in scope, since one compares States and UTs within India while the other compares countries.

quizzes.title: Pokhran and the 1998 milestones
quizzes.passage: National Technology Day is observed every year on 11 May. The day commemorates technological achievements reached on 11 May 1998, when several milestones were reached. One of these was a series of nuclear tests conducted at the Pokhran Test Range in Rajasthan. India had earlier carried out a nuclear test at the same range, and the 1998 tests marked a major step in the country's scientific history. Students preparing for current affairs should be clear about the sequence of these events, the people who led them, and the names given to the operations. The 1998 tests were not the only technological milestones of that day. Another was the first successful test flight of the Hansa-3 aircraft, which marked progress in indigenous aviation. The Defence Research and Development Organisation also carried out a test of the Trishul missile, a short-range surface-to-air weapon. Together these events show why the day is linked with self-reliance in technology. The day has been observed every year since the government began marking it in 1999. quizzes.title: Constitution and labour laws: practice set
quizzes.passage: Labour welfare in India is shaped by two sources of authority: the Constitution and a body of ordinary statutes. The Constitution does not only grant rights to individuals; it also sets out aims that the State is expected to pursue. Some provisions protect workers from being made to work against their will, while others shield young people from early employment. Other provisions describe the kind of economic life the State should aim for, including a means of livelihood, employment within economic capacity, fair pay and a voice for workers in the industries where they work. Statutes have translated many of these aims into laws covering factories, wages, provident funds, compensation and disputes between employers and employees. Several of these statutes have since been grouped into a smaller number of broad codes. The codes group rules on wages, industrial relations, social security and occupational safety and health. Each statute addresses a specific aspect of work, such as the payment of wages, the settlement of disputes or compensation to workers. Labour matters also have an international dimension, since a United Nations agency works to improve labour conditions and living standards across the world. Together, these provisions and laws show that labour protection in India has both a constitutional foundation and a statutory one.

quizzes.title: ILO: short answer set
quizzes.passage: Some international bodies are created to set common standards rather than to govern countries directly. The organisation has four stated objectives. It seeks to promote fundamental labour rights, create greater opportunities for women and men, enhance social protection and strengthen social dialogue. Its legal instruments take two forms. Conventions and Protocols are legally binding treaties, while Recommendations are non-binding guidelines. Some of its standards form part of the wider United Nations human rights framework. The organisation also publishes reports on employment, wages, social protection and youth. Its Director General leads the organisation's work. The work covers workers in many countries, including India, which is one of its founding members. quizzes.title: ASEAN Basics and Forums
quizzes.passage: Southeast Asia is home to a regional grouping that has become central to how countries in the region manage their relations with one another and with major outside powers. Leaders and ministers meet through a network of regional forums that cover trade, politics and security, and several of these meetings now include partners from outside the region. The group has also tried to deepen economic ties, aiming to make trade, investment and the movement of people easier across national borders. Its record is not without difficulty. A dispute over a busy sea route has remained unresolved for years, and the group has been criticised for its limited response to a political crisis inside one of its member states. For India, the region has a special importance. New Delhi has built deep political, economic and security ties with the grouping over many years, and its own regional outreach policy places the grouping at the heart of its approach to the wider Indo-Pacific. quizzes.title: RBI Surplus and Capital Framework
quizzes.passage: The Reserve Bank of India earns income from its operations, and every year it decides how much of that income to keep and how much to pass on to the central government. The rules for these decisions are set out in a framework known as the Economic Capital Framework, which tells the bank how to provide for financial risks and how to transfer its surplus. A surplus is the net income left after total expenditure is deducted from total income. The bank earns this income from buying and selling bonds in the market, from the interest it receives on bonds it holds, and from returns on its foreign currency assets. To guard against unexpected losses, such as falls in the value of securities or the effects of changes in interest rates, the bank maintains a contingency buffer. The surplus is handed over to the government only after this buffer has reached its target level. The bank's board has recently approved a record transfer to the government, and the framework itself has been reviewed by expert committees over time. Analysts see these transfers as helping the government with its finances, reducing its borrowing needs and supporting its spending on infrastructure.

quizzes.title: Governance and Parliamentary Oversight
quizzes.passage: Governance in India is judged at several levels, and each level has tools to measure performance. At the village level, a national framework assesses how well local bodies deliver rural services. Rather than offering a simple ranking, it places each body into a category based on a composite score, so officials can see where improvement is needed. Government statistics agencies run regular surveys of economic activity, including enterprises that are not registered as companies. Such data is useful for planning because it captures sectors that formal records often miss. Finally, oversight of public money rests with Parliament. A committee drawn from both Houses examines how the government spends money and studies reports prepared by the country's audit institution. Its members are chosen in a way that reflects the balance of political parties, which gives the committee its credibility. This oversight protects financial discipline in public spending. A new mission from a European space agency and a partner from East Asia studies this interaction. It captures images in two kinds of light at the same time and tracks how the solar flow meets the magnetic shield in near real time. quizzes.title: CJI Appointment and Collegium Rulings
quizzes.passage: The appointment of judges to the Supreme Court has been a subject of repeated litigation in India, and the Court has ruled on it several times. For a long period after the Court was set up, the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court was generally appointed Chief Justice of India. This practice was set aside twice in the 1970s, when the government chose judges who were not the seniormost. The Constitution requires the President to consult certain persons before appointing judges, and the meaning of the word consultation became a dispute. The First Judges Case of 1981 examined this word. The Second Judges Case of 1993 later revisited the question of how the Chief Justice of India should be chosen. The Third Judges Case of 1998 dealt with the process that the Chief Justice must follow before sending recommendations to the Government. Parliament later sought to replace the collegium with a new body, the National Judicial Appointments Commission, through a constitutional amendment and an Act. The Fourth Judges Case of 2015 examined that amendment and the Act. The rulings are known as the First, Second, Third and Fourth Judges Cases. The 1973 and 1977 appointments were made by the government of the time.

quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of India exercises more than one kind of jurisdiction. It hears appeals against decisions of lower courts, decides certain disputes at the first instance, and gives advice when asked. A person whose Fundamental Rights have been violated may approach the Court directly, which gives the Court a role beyond routine appeals. The President of India can also refer questions of public importance to the Court. The Constitution provides for situations in which the Court may need a temporary head or additional judges. One provision deals with the office of the Chief Justice of India when that office is vacant or cannot be filled, while others allow the Chief Justice to draw on judges who are not part of the regular bench. Such provisions are meant for specific circumstances and carry their own conditions. Some of these arrangements involve a retired judge or a High Court judge. The Court's jurisdiction is therefore divided into several parts, each set out in the Constitution. The arrangements described above allow the Court to continue its work when its regular composition is incomplete or its head is unavailable. Each of these provisions is a separate route, and a reader must know which one applies to a given situation.

quizzes.passage: A legislator does not lose membership simply because he or she disagrees with a colleague or a party leader. The rules on loss of membership are set out as a list of specific grounds, and the list covers both a member's conduct and his or her personal circumstances. Some grounds relate to choices a member makes in connection with a political party. Others relate to the member's status and to certain personal circumstances. Decisions on these grounds are made by the presiding officer of the house. A ground must be clearly made out before a seat can be lost, and the rules do not treat every political disagreement as a reason to remove a member. The grounds are set out in the Constitution and in the law itself, so the presiding officer applies a fixed checklist rather than an open-ended power. Membership of a legislature therefore depends on whether one of the listed grounds applies, and the booklet describes the grounds in some detail for this reason. When a listed ground is found to apply, the member can lose the seat. quizzes.title: How the Press Freedom Index Works
quizzes.passage: Press freedom refers to the ability of journalists to gather information and publish it without undue pressure. Conditions for this differ widely from one country to another, and the World Press Freedom Index compares them within a single framework. The index ranks countries and regions according to the level of freedom available to journalists. To reach this ranking, it evaluates several aspects of the media environment, including how varied the media are, how independent they remain, and how well the legal system supports them. A central tool in this work is a questionnaire that gathers information on the conditions in which reporters operate. The results are released in a published report that places each country on a list and allows readers to compare nations with one another. Because the report reflects conditions at the time of assessment, a country's position can change when its situation changes. A free press is also described as one that acts independently, promotes transparency and holds powerful people accountable. Journalism therefore has a role beyond the newsroom, since it can give a voice to those who lack institutional power and can highlight injustices that would otherwise go unseen. For this reason, the index serves as a measure of how well journalists are able to do their work.

quizzes.title: Press Freedom: Challenges and Role
quizzes.passage: Press freedom is shaped by a number of pressures, and financial strain is among the most widely noted. Media outlets in many countries face financial instability, which can threaten independent and unbiased reporting. Freedom of expression is regarded as vital to preserve journalistic integrity and to prevent undue influence from state or private actors. A free press is described as one that acts independently, promotes transparency and holds powerful people accountable. Its work reaches beyond the newsroom, since it highlights systemic injustices and enables public participation in democratic discourse through information, critique and civic dialogue. News coverage can also influence discussions in parliamentary and legislative bodies. A widely quoted line makes a similar point in a few words: where the press is free, and every man able to read, all is safe. These roles explain why the press is treated as significant in public life. Taken together, the pressures on the press and the roles it plays help explain why its condition matters to a society as a whole. Independence, transparency and accountability are therefore the qualities by which such a press is described. Freedom of the press is linked to a range of functions, from informing the public to examining those in power.

LEADS is India's national index for benchmarking logistics performance across the States and Union Territories of India. It evaluates each State and UT across key logistics parameters, including infrastructure, service quality, regulatory environment, operational efficiency and data-driven logistics reforms.

The 2025 edition introduced a four-tier classification system in place of the earlier model. Each entry also carries a regional tag, and the tags used in the report are Coastal, Landlocked, North-East (N-E) and UTs. The regional tag appears next to each name in these lists.

The Thucydides Trap is a phrase used in international relations to describe the danger of conflict when a rising power challenges a power that is already dominant. The idea comes from the writings of Thucydides, who analysed a long war between two rival powers. Its core idea is that fear and rivalry between powers can make a clash more likely, and the concept is often discussed in relation to a rising power and an existing global power. Critics argue that the idea oversimplifies politics by suggesting conflict is unavoidable, while others stress that diplomacy and economic links can prevent escalation.

The World Health Organization has declared an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo to be a serious international health emergency. Under the International Health Regulations, such a declaration applies when a health risk could spread across borders and needs a coordinated response. Ebola is a severe viral disease that can affect humans and primates.

Ecocide refers to unlawful or reckless acts that cause severe, widespread or long-term environmental damage, carried out with knowledge that such damage is likely. The idea has gained legal attention, and several countries have written it into their own laws, which is one reason it is discussed in environmental debates.
